Robert Walpole. Recognized as Britain's first Prime Minister, he dominated Parliament for over two decades under George I and George II, establishing the principle that the Crown's chief minister must command the confidence of the House of Commons.

Walpole served as First Lord of the Treasury for nearly twenty-one years, from 1721 to 1742, the longest tenure of any British Prime Minister. He rose to prominence as a Whig during the South Sea Bubble crisis, steering clear of financial disaster that ruined rivals and positioning himself as a safe pair of hands.

Walpole cultivated George I and George II by accepting the Crown's reduced role in day-to-day governance, allowing the monarch to cede power to Cabinet ministers. This was a revolutionary shift in how the British state operated. He mastered the art of parliamentary patronage and corruption, rewarding allies with titles, pensions, and sinecures to maintain a reliable majority in the House.

He promoted financial stability and avoided costly foreign wars, earning the epithet "the Minister of Peace." His government set the template for constitutional monarchy that endured for centuries. His resignation in 1742 over the War of Jenkins's Ear marked the beginning of the end of his dominance, yet his legacy shaped how British politics would function for generations to come.
